questions.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(3t-2)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t+6)\underset{\sim}{j}$. What is its displacement from $t=2$ to $t=6$?

options.why: Subtracted the later position from the earlier one instead of the other way round.
Added the two position vectors instead of subtracting them.
Gave the position at $t=6$ rather than the change in position.

questions.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}+t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t-7)\underset{\sim}{j}$. What is its displacement from $t=1$ to $t=4$?

options.why: Subtracted the later position from the earlier one instead of the other way round.
Added the two position vectors instead of subtracting them.
Gave the position at $t=4$ rather than the change in position.

questions.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=5t\underset{\sim}{i}+4t^{2}\underset{\sim}{j}$. How far apart are its positions at $t=1$ and $t=2$?

options.why: Added the components $5+12$ instead of using Pythagoras.
Subtracted the components $12-5$ instead of using Pythagoras.
Found $5^{2}+12^{2}$ but did not take the square root.

questions.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}+t)\underset{\sim}{j}$. What angle does its displacement from $t=1$ to $t=3$ make with the positive $x$-axis, measured anticlockwise to the nearest degree?

options.why: Used $\tan\theta=\frac{6}{10}$, dividing the horizontal change by the vertical change.
Subtracted the angle from $180^{\circ}$, as if the displacement pointed left.
Measured the angle clockwise from the positive $x$-axis instead of anticlockwise.

questions.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=t^{2}\underset{\sim}{i}+7t\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$. Its displacement from $t=3$ to a later time $T$ is $40\underset{\sim}{i}+28\underset{\sim}{j}$. What is $T$?

options.why: Found the change in time, $28\div7$, but did not add it to $t=3$.
Treated the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ component $40$ as a change in time and added it to $3$.
Treated the $\underset{\sim}{j}$ component $28$ as a change in time and added it to $3$.

questions.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=5\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+5\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$. What is its displacement from $t=0$ to $t=\pi$?

options.why: Subtracted the later position from the earlier one instead of the other way round.
Used $\sin\pi=1$ instead of $\sin\pi=0$.
Used $\cos\pi=0$ instead of $\cos\pi=-1$.

questions.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=4\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+4\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$. What is the exact distance between its positions at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$?

options.why: Used $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=-\frac{1}{2}$, which makes the vertical change $4$ instead of $0$.
Saw that both positions have $y=2$ and concluded they were the same point.
Used only the first position's $x$-coordinate as the horizontal change, taking the second position to be on the $y$-axis.

questions.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=2t\underset{\sim}{i}+(9-t^{2})\underset{\sim}{j}$. What angle does its displacement from $t=1$ to $t=4$ make with the positive $x$-axis, measured anticlockwise to the nearest degree?

options.why: Ignored the negative $\underset{\sim}{j}$ component and gave the first-quadrant angle.
Added $180^{\circ}$, placing the displacement in the third quadrant instead of the fourth.
Subtracted from $180^{\circ}$, placing the displacement in the second quadrant instead of the fourth.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{r}(1)=2\underset{\sim}{i}+8\underset{\sim}{j}$
$\underset{\sim}{r}(4)=8\underset{\sim}{i}-7\underset{\sim}{j}$
$\underset{\sim}{r}(4)-\underset{\sim}{r}(1)=6\underset{\sim}{i}-15\underset{\sim}{j}$
The displacement points right and down, so it lies in the fourth quadrant.
$\tan^{-1}\dfrac{15}{6}=68^{\circ}$
$\theta=360^{\circ}-68^{\circ}$
$=292^{\circ}$
